title: V. Not You, Not You!
paragraphs: On his way to Ivan’s, Alyosha had to walk past the house where Katerina Ivanovna lived. Lights were burning in the windows. He stopped short and decided to go in. He had not seen Katerina Ivanovna in over a week. Now it struck him that Ivan might be with her, especially with that terrible day so close. He rang, and started up the staircase, which was dimly lit by a Chinese lantern. A man was coming down. As they passed, he recognized his brother. So Ivan was just leaving Katerina Ivanovna’s.
“Oh, it’s only you,” said Ivan drily. “Well, goodbye. You’re going up to see her?”
“Yes.”
“I wouldn’t, if I were you. She’s upset, and you’ll only upset her more.”
Just then a door upstairs banged open, and a voice cried out:
“No, no! Alexey Fyodorovitch, are you coming from him?”
“Yes, I’ve been with him.”
“Has he sent me any message? Come up, Alyosha. And you, Ivan Fyodorovitch, you have to come back. You must. Do you hear?”
Katya’s voice was so peremptory that Ivan hesitated for a moment, then made up his mind to go back up with Alyosha.
“She was listening at the door,” he muttered to himself in anger, but Alyosha heard him.
“Forgive me for keeping my greatcoat on,” said Ivan as he entered the drawing-room. “I won’t sit down. I’m not staying more than a minute.”

“Do sit down, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” said Katerina Ivanovna, although she herself remained standing. She had changed very little over those weeks, but there was an ominous glint in her dark eyes. Alyosha remembered later that she had struck him then as especially beautiful.
“What did he ask you to tell me?”

“Just one thing,” said Alyosha, looking her straight in the face. “He asks you to spare yourself, and at the trial not to speak about what” (he faltered a little) “... went on between you ... when you first met ... in that town.”

“Ha! The fact that I bowed to the ground before him for that money!” She gave a bitter laugh. “So which is he afraid for, me or himself? He asks me to spare—who? Him, or myself? Tell me, Alexey Fyodorovitch!”
Alyosha studied her intently, trying to understand.
“You and him both,” he answered quietly.
“Well, I’m glad to hear it,” she snapped spitefully, and all at once she flushed.
“You don’t know me yet, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she said, almost threatening. “I don’t know myself yet, either. After I’ve been examined tomorrow, you may want to trample me underfoot.”
“You’ll give your evidence honorably,” said Alyosha. “That’s all anyone asks.”

“Women are often dishonorable,” she snarled. “Only an hour ago I was thinking how I was afraid even to touch that monster ... as if he were some reptile ... and yet no, to me he’s still a human being! But did he do it? Is he the murderer?” she suddenly cried out, hysterical, wheeling round on Ivan. Alyosha saw at once that she had put this same question to Ivan before, perhaps only a moment before he walked in, and not for the first time but the hundredth, and that they had ended up quarreling.

“I went to see Smerdyakov.... You were the one, you persuaded me that he murdered his father. I believed no one but you!” she went on, still speaking to Ivan. He answered with a strained sort of smile. Her tone made Alyosha start. He had never guessed that they were on such familiar, intimate terms.
“Well, that’s enough of that,” Ivan said, cutting the talk short. “I’m going. I’ll be back tomorrow.” With that he turned on his heel, left the room and went straight down the stairs.
Katerina Ivanovna imperiously seized both of Alyosha’s hands.

“Go after him! Catch him! Don’t leave him alone, not for a minute!” she said in a quick whisper. “He’s mad! Don’t you know he’s mad? He has a fever, a nervous fever. The doctor told me. Go on, run after him....”
Alyosha jumped up and ran after Ivan, who was not yet fifty paces ahead.
“What do you want?” Ivan wheeled on him when he saw he was being chased. “She told you to catch me, because I’m mad. I know the whole speech by heart,” he added irritably.
“She’s wrong, of course. But she’s right that you’re ill,” said Alyosha. “I was watching your face just now. You look very ill, Ivan.”
Ivan kept walking and did not stop. Alyosha followed.
“Do you know, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how it happens that people lose their minds?” Ivan asked. His voice had suddenly gone quiet, with no trace of irritation, and sounded merely curious.
“No, I don’t. I suppose there are all sorts of ways.”
“And can a man notice for himself that he’s going mad?”
“I imagine he can’t see himself clearly at such a time,” Alyosha answered, surprised.
Ivan said nothing for half a minute.
“If you want to talk to me, change the subject,” he said abruptly.

“Oh, I almost forgot, I have a letter for you,” said Alyosha timidly. He took Lise’s note out of his pocket and held it out to Ivan. They were just under a street lamp. Ivan knew the handwriting at once.
“Ah, from that little demon!” he laughed maliciously. Without opening the envelope, he tore it to pieces and tossed them into the air. The wind blew the scraps away.
“Not even sixteen yet, I believe, and she’s already throwing herself at men,” he said with contempt, and strode on down the street.
“What do you mean, throwing herself?” Alyosha exclaimed.
“The way loose women do, naturally.”

“How can you say that, Ivan, how can you?” Alyosha cried hotly, in a grieved voice. “She’s a child! You’re insulting a child! She’s ill, she’s very ill. She may be close to madness herself.... I had hoped to hear something from you ... something that would save her.”
“You’ll hear nothing from me. If she’s a child, I’m not her nurse. Be quiet, Alexey. Don’t keep on about her. I’m not even thinking about it.”
For a moment they walked on in silence again.
“She’ll spend the whole night praying to the Mother of God to show her what to do tomorrow at the trial,” he said, again sharp and angry.
“You ... you mean Katerina Ivanovna?”

“Yes. Whether to save Mitya or destroy him. She’ll pray to be shown the way. She can’t make up her own mind, you see. She hasn’t had time to decide yet. She takes me for her nurse, too. She wants me to sing her to sleep.”
“Katerina Ivanovna loves you, brother,” said Alyosha sadly.
“Maybe so. I’m not very taken with her.”

“She’s suffering. So why do you ... sometimes say things to her that give her hope?” Alyosha went on, with timid reproach. “I know you have given her hope. Forgive me for talking to you like this,” he added.

“I can’t treat her as I should—break with her once and for all and tell her so to her face,” said Ivan irritably. “I have to wait until the murderer’s sentence has been passed. If I break with her now, she’ll get her revenge on me tomorrow by destroying that scoundrel at the trial. She hates him, and she knows she hates him. It’s all a lie—lie on top of lie! As long as I haven’t broken with her, she keeps hoping, and she won’t destroy that monster, because she knows how badly I want to get him off. If only that damned verdict would come!”
The words “murderer” and “monster” rang painfully in Alyosha’s heart.
“But how could she destroy Mitya?” he asked, turning Ivan’s words over in his mind. “What can she testify that would ruin Mitya?”
“You don’t know yet. She holds a document, written in Mitya’s own hand, that proves beyond question that he did murder Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
“That’s impossible!” cried Alyosha.
“Why impossible? I’ve read it myself.”
“There can’t be any such document!” Alyosha insisted hotly. “There can’t, because he is not the murderer. It was not he who killed father, not he!”
Ivan stopped abruptly.
“Then who is the murderer, according to you?” he asked, with an air of coldness. His voice even had a note of disdain.
“You know who,” said Alyosha, in a low voice that pierced.
“Who? You mean that fairy tale about the crazy idiot, the epileptic, Smerdyakov?”
Alyosha felt himself begin to shake from head to foot.
“You know who,” escaped him helplessly. He could hardly breathe.
“Who? Who?” Ivan cried, almost savagely. All his self-control was suddenly gone.
“I know only one thing,” Alyosha went on, still almost whispering, “_it wasn’t you_ who killed father.”
“‘Not you’! What do you mean, ‘not you’?” Ivan was stunned.
“It was not you who killed father. Not you!” Alyosha said again, firmly.
Neither spoke for half a minute.
“I know I didn’t. Are you out of your head?” said Ivan, with a pale, crooked smile. He stared fixedly at Alyosha. They were standing under a lamp-post again.
“No, Ivan. You have told yourself several times that you are the murderer.”
“When did I ever say that? I was in Moscow.... When did I say it?” Ivan stammered, helpless.

“You’ve said it to yourself many times, all alone, through these two dreadful months,” Alyosha went on, as softly and clearly as before. Yet he seemed to be speaking now not for himself, not of his own will, but under some irresistible command. “You have accused yourself. You have admitted to yourself that you are the murderer and no one else. But you didn’t do it. You are mistaken. You are not the murderer. Do you hear me? It was not you! God sent me to tell you so.”
Both were silent. The silence lasted a whole long minute. They stood motionless, looking into each other’s eyes. Both were pale. Then Ivan began shaking all over and gripped Alyosha by the shoulder.
“You’ve been in my room!” he whispered hoarsely. “You were there in the night, when he came.... Admit it ... have you seen him, have you seen him?”
“Who? Do you mean Mitya?” Alyosha asked, bewildered.
“Not him, damn the monster!” Ivan shouted, frantic. “Do you know that he comes to see me? How did you find out? Tell me!”
“Who is _he_? I don’t know who you mean,” Alyosha faltered, growing alarmed.
“Yes, you do know ... or how could you—? You can’t possibly not know.”
Then he seemed to stop himself. He stood still, apparently thinking. A strange grin twisted his mouth.

“Brother,” Alyosha began again, in a trembling voice, “I said this to you because I know you’ll believe what I say. I’m telling you once and for all: it’s not you. Do you hear, once and for all! God put it into my heart to tell you, even if it makes you hate me from this hour on.”
But by now Ivan had evidently pulled himself together.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch,” he said with a cold smile, “I can’t stand prophets and epileptics—messengers from God above all—and you know that only too well. From this moment I cut off all relations with you, and probably for good. Leave me at this turning, please. It’s the way to your lodgings as well. And take particular care not to come to me today! Do you hear?”
He turned and walked on with a steady step, without looking back.
“Brother,” Alyosha called after him, “if anything happens to you today, come to me before anyone else!”

But Ivan did not answer. Alyosha stood under the lamp-post at the crossroads until Ivan had disappeared into the dark. Then he turned and walked slowly home. Both Alyosha and Ivan lived in lodgings, since neither would live in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s empty house. Alyosha rented a furnished room from some working people. Ivan lived some distance off. He had taken a roomy, fairly comfortable lodge attached to a fine house, owned by a well-to-do lady, an official’s widow. His only servant was a deaf, rheumatic old crone who went to bed at six every evening and rose at six every morning. Ivan had lately become remarkably careless of comfort, and very fond of solitude. He did everything for himself in the single room he lived in, and he seldom set foot in any other room of the lodge.

He came to the gate of the house and already had his hand on the bell when he suddenly stopped. He realized he was shaking all over with rage. All at once he let go of the bell, turned back with a curse and hurried off in the opposite direction. He walked a mile and a half to a tiny, crooked wooden house, little better than a hut. Marya Kondratyevna was now lodging there. She was the neighbor who used to come to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s kitchen for soup, and Smerdyakov had once sung his songs to her and played the guitar. She had sold their little house and now lived here with her mother. Smerdyakov, who was ill—almost dying—had been with them ever since Fyodor Pavlovitch’s death. Ivan was going to see him now, driven by a sudden, irresistible impulse.
